title: Solving Congruences
references: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, eighth edition, Section 4.4, printed pages 290–300.
Original companion explanations, examples, diagrams, executable demonstrations, and practice checks.

units.title: Replace division by multiplication with an inverse

blocks.notation:
u is an inverse of a modulo m if au ≡ 1 (mod m), with m > 1.
An inverse exists exactly when gcd(a,m) = 1.
blocks.description: The inverse is unique as a residue class modulo m, not as a single integer.

blocks.text: If gcd(a,m) = 1, Bézout gives sa + tm = 1. Reducing modulo m gives sa ≡ 1, so s is an inverse. Conversely, au ≡ 1 means au − km = 1 for some integer k. Every common divisor of a,m must then divide 1, so their gcd is 1.

For uniqueness, suppose au ≡ av ≡ 1 (mod m). Since a is coprime to m, cancellation gives u ≡ v (mod m). Thus exactly one inverse lies in 0 through m − 1; all other inverse integers differ from it by multiples of m.

blocks.prompt: Why does 6 have no inverse modulo 15, even though you can divide by 6 over the real numbers?

explanation.text: gcd(6,15) = 3. An equation 6u − 15k = 1 would have a left side divisible by 3 and a right side not divisible by 3. A real reciprocal is a different object.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.1–§4.4.2, pp. 290–291.

units.title: Read an inverse from the correct Bézout coefficient

blocks.text: The coefficient of 17 is −5, so the inverse is −5 mod 43 = 38. Check: 17·38 = 646 = 43·15 + 1.
Check the original equation: 17·27 = 459 = 43·10 + 29. Every integer x = 27 + 43k works, and inverse cancellation shows there are no other solution classes.

blocks.prompt: Could 2, the other Bézout coefficient above, be the inverse of 17 modulo 43?

explanation.text: No. It multiplies 43 in the identity, so it disappears when reducing modulo 43. Use the coefficient attached to the number whose inverse you need.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.2, pp. 292–293.

units.title: Return an inverse only when the gcd permits one

blocks.text: The functions here reuse extendedGcd from Section 4.3; paste that definition first. They accept exact BigInt inputs. normalizedMod returns a nonnegative remainder. inverseMod returns the canonical inverse or null when none exists; it requires m > 1.

blocks.description: Executable JavaScript depending on extendedGcd. inverseMod(17n,43n) returns 38n; inverseMod(6n,15n) returns null.

blocks.text: A missing inverse does not automatically mean a linear congruence has no solution. It means the coefficient cannot be canceled while keeping the same modulus. The next unit checks whether the right side shares the necessary divisor.

blocks.prompt: What is inverseMod(-17n,43n), and how can you check it?

explanation.text: It is 5n because (−17)·5 = −85 = 43·(−2) + 1. A negative coefficient is normalized to its residue representative.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.2, pp. 291–293; executable companion demonstration.

units.title: Reduce by the gcd and retain every solution class

blocks.notation:
For ax ≡ b (mod m), let g = gcd(a,m), m > 0.
If g does not divide b: no solution.
If g divides b: (a/g)x ≡ b/g (mod m/g).
blocks.description: Dividing the equation ax − b = km by g changes the coefficient, right side, and modulus together.

blocks.text: When g divides b, the reduced coefficient is coprime to the reduced modulus. Solve the reduced congruence. If x₀ is its canonical solution and h = m/g, all integer solutions are x = x₀ + kh. There are exactly g distinct residue solutions modulo the original m: x₀, x₀ + h, …, x₀ + (g − 1)h.
Solve 18x ≡ 12 (mod 30). Here g = 6 divides 12. Reduce to 3x ≡ 2 (mod 5). The inverse of 3 modulo 5 is 2, so x ≡ 4 (mod 5).
The six residues modulo 30 are 4,9,14,19,24,29. For 18x ≡ 13 (mod 30), the same gcd 6 does not divide 13, so there is no solution.

blocks.description: Executable JavaScript reusing extendedGcd and normalizedMod. It returns null or {base,period,count}; all solutions are base + k*period, and count is the number of classes modulo the original m.

blocks.text: The Bézout coefficient s obeys s(a/g) + t(m/g) = 1, so it supplies the reduced inverse directly. If the reduced modulus is 1, every integer works and the function returns base 0, period 1. This handles 0x ≡ 0 (mod m), and also any congruence modulo 1, without asking inverseMod to invert modulo 1.

blocks.prompt: Solve 0x ≡ 5 (mod 5) and 0x ≡ 1 (mod 5).

explanation.text: The first is true for every integer x, represented by period 1. The second has no solution. The zero coefficient does not justify division by zero.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.2, pp. 291–293; companion extension for noninvertible coefficients.

A system asks one integer x to satisfy several congruences at once. The Chinese remainder theorem says: if the moduli m₁,…,mₙ are pairwise relatively prime and each exceeds 1, there is exactly one solution residue modulo M = m₁m₂…mₙ for every list of target remainders.

blocks.description: The moduli 4,5,7 are pairwise coprime even though 4 is not prime.

blocks.title: One residue satisfies three clocks
blocks.description: The integer 51 leaves remainders 3,1,2 modulo 4,5,7. Adding 140 preserves all three remainders.

blocks.text: “Unique modulo 140” does not mean only one integer solution. The canonical solution is 51, while all integer solutions are 51 + 140k for k ∈ ℤ. A separate range restriction would select a particular integer.

blocks.prompt: Does an overall gcd of 1 for moduli 6,10,15 suffice for this theorem?

explanation.text: No. The theorem requires pairwise coprimality. Those moduli share factors in every pair.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.3, pp. 293–294.

units.title: Build a term that selects one congruence at a time

blocks.text: Set Mᵢ = M/mᵢ. This number is divisible by all the other moduli. Find yᵢ with Mᵢyᵢ ≡ 1 (mod mᵢ). Then Eᵢ = Mᵢyᵢ is 1 in coordinate i and 0 in every other coordinate. Multiply Eᵢ by the desired remainder aᵢ and add.

blocks.notation:
x = Σ aᵢMᵢyᵢ mod M
x = (315 + 56 + 240) mod 140 = 51
blocks.description: When viewed modulo mᵢ, all terms except term i vanish, and that remaining term gives aᵢ.

blocks.text: Uniqueness needs its own argument. If x and z satisfy every congruence, each mᵢ divides x − z. Since these moduli are pairwise coprime, their prime factors do not overlap, so their product M divides x − z. Hence x ≡ z (mod M). This uses prime factorization, not the uniqueness claim being proved.

blocks.prompt: Why can 35 be inverted modulo 4, while it vanishes modulo 5 and modulo 7?

explanation.text: 35 is coprime to 4, and 35·3 = 105 leaves 1 modulo 4. It is divisible by 5 and 7, so every multiple of 35 leaves 0 under those moduli.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.3, pp. 294–295.

units.title: Merge congruences by substituting an integer parameter

blocks.title: Solve the same system by substitution

blocks.text: From x ≡ 3 (mod 4), write x = 3 + 4t. The second congruence gives 3 + 4t ≡ 1 (mod 5), so 4t ≡ 3 and t ≡ 2 (mod 5).
Write t = 2 + 5u. Then x = 3 + 4(2 + 5u) = 11 + 20u.
Use the third congruence: 11 + 20u ≡ 2 (mod 7), hence 6u ≡ 5. Because 6 is its own inverse modulo 7, u ≡ 2 (mod 7).
Write u = 2 + 7v. Then x = 11 + 20(2 + 7v) = 51 + 140v. This is the same solution class as the construction.

Every substitution uses a fresh integer parameter. Keep the equation form until the system is fully merged, then translate it back into a congruence. This helps avoid silently losing possible solutions.

blocks.prompt: Why is x = 11 + 20u already enough to satisfy the first two conditions?

explanation.text: Modulo 4, 11 gives 3 and 20u gives 0. Modulo 5, 11 gives 1 and 20u gives 0. Only the third condition remains to determine u modulo 7.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.3, p. 295.

units.title: Implement the construction with checked moduli

blocks.text: This function reuses extendedGcd, normalizedMod, and inverseMod. Each input row contains BigInt fields residue and modulus. It accepts noncanonical or negative target residues, but requires a nonempty array and pairwise coprime moduli greater than 1.

The inverse check also validates pairwise coprimality: gcd(M/mᵢ,mᵢ) = 1 for every i exactly when no two moduli share a prime divisor. The returned residue is in [0,M), and all solutions differ by a multiple of M. Rejected moduli do not prove a system inconsistent; they mean this particular implementation’s assumptions are not met.

blocks.prompt: What should the function do with moduli 6 and 9, even if both target remainders are 0?

explanation.text: Reject those moduli because they are not coprime. That system does have solutions, but it requires a method that handles shared factors.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.3, pp. 294–295; executable companion demonstration.

units.title: Check compatibility when the moduli share a divisor

blocks.notation:
x ≡ a (mod m), x ≡ b (mod n) is solvable iff gcd(m,n) | (b − a).
When solvable, solutions form one class modulo lcm(m,n).
blocks.description: This two-equation extension allows shared factors; m and n are positive.

blocks.text: Proof: put x = a + mt into the second congruence. You obtain mt ≡ b − a (mod n), which the general linear criterion solves exactly when gcd(m,n) divides b − a. Its parameter period is n/g, so the resulting x period is mn/g = lcm(m,n).
For x ≡ 2 (mod 6), x ≡ 5 (mod 9), the difference is 3 and gcd(6,9) = 3. Write x = 2 + 6t; then 6t ≡ 3 (mod 9), so 2t ≡ 1 (mod 3) and t ≡ 2. Thus x ≡ 14 (mod 18).
If the second target is 4 instead, the difference is 2, which is not divisible by 3. There is no solution.

blocks.prompt: Why would “unique modulo 54” be misleading in the compatible example?

explanation.text: The true period is 18. There are three solutions in [0,54): 14,32,50. The product period overcounts when the moduli share factors.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.3 and exercise themes, pp. 294–295, 302; companion extension.

units.title: Recover an integer only within the declared range

blocks.text: With moduli 4,5,7, encode an integer a by (a mod 4,a mod 5,a mod 7). CRT recovers its residue modulo 140. If you know 0 ≤ a < 140, that determines the actual integer uniquely. Without a bound, many integers have the same tuple.

Compute componentwise and reduce each coordinate under its own modulus. The product is actually 368, but its tuple is also the tuple of 88 because 368 − 88 = 2·140. To recover 368 as an exact nonnegative result, choose a product of moduli strictly larger than the possible result before computing.

The coordinate calculations can be done independently. Their stored residues are small, but temporary products may approach the square of a coordinate modulus; reconstruction also uses larger integers. Special moduli 2ᵏ − 1 can simplify binary reductions. Pairwise coprime exponents, such as 2,3,5, give pairwise coprime moduli 3,7,31 because gcd(2ᵘ − 1,2ᵛ − 1) = 2^gcd(u,v) − 1.

blocks.prompt: Why must the known range be half-open, 0 ≤ a < M, rather than 0 ≤ a ≤ M?

explanation.text: Both 0 and M have all-zero remainder tuples. Including both endpoints would destroy uniqueness.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.4, pp. 295–297.

units.title: Keep the prime-modulus and nonzero-base hypotheses

blocks.notation:
If p is prime and p does not divide a, then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
For every integer a, aᵖ ≡ a (mod p).
blocks.description: Fermat’s little theorem is different from Fermat’s last theorem. The first form excludes bases divisible by p; the second form does not.

blocks.text: To see why the first form holds, multiply residues 1,2,…,p − 1 by a. None becomes 0, and no two collide: cancellation is valid because gcd(a,p) = 1. Thus the products are a rearrangement of the same nonzero residues. Multiplying them gives a^(p−1)(p − 1)! ≡ (p − 1)!. The factorial is coprime to p, so cancel it.
Multiply by a to obtain aᵖ ≡ a when p does not divide a. If p divides a, both aᵖ and a are 0 modulo p, so the second form still holds.

blocks.prompt: Can you conclude 13¹² ≡ 1 (mod 13)?

explanation.text: No: 13 divides the base. The left side is 0 modulo 13. The universally valid form gives 13¹³ ≡ 13 ≡ 0 instead.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.5, pp. 297–298.

units.title: Reduce exponents modulo p minus one when permitted

blocks.text: The modulus 13 is prime and does not divide 5. Fermat gives 5¹² ≡ 1. Divide the exponent: 123 = 10·12 + 3.
Then 5¹²³ = (5¹²)¹⁰·5³ ≡ 125 ≡ 8 (mod 13). The exponent is reduced modulo 12, while the result is reduced modulo 13.

blocks.notation: a⁻¹ ≡ a^(p−2) (mod p), if p is prime and p does not divide a.
blocks.description: Multiplying this candidate by a gives a^(p−1) ≡ 1. The notation a⁻¹ means a modular inverse, not a real reciprocal.

blocks.text: For composite moduli, this particular exponent shortcut is not justified. Section 4.2’s repeated-squaring algorithm works for any positive modulus without assuming primality. It also handles a base divisible by the modulus, using the stated exponent-zero convention.

blocks.prompt: Why is reducing the exponent of 13¹² modulo 12 invalid modulo 13?

explanation.text: It would replace a positive exponent by 0 and change a residue of 0 into 1. The required condition that 13 not divide the base fails.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.5, pp. 297–298.

units.title: Use a failed Fermat test as evidence of compositeness

blocks.text: For n > 1 and a base a coprime to n, every prime n satisfies a^(n−1) ≡ 1 (mod n). If the congruence fails, n is composite. If it passes, n may still be composite. A composite n that passes for a positive base a is a pseudoprime to that base.

blocks.title: A passing result that is not a prime certificate

blocks.text: 341 = 11·31 is composite. Yet 2¹⁰ = 1024 = 3·341 + 1, so 2³⁴⁰ = (2¹⁰)³⁴ ≡ 1 (mod 341). It passes the base-2 Fermat test.
A different base can expose it: repeated squaring gives 3³⁴⁰ mod 341 = 56, not 1. Thus base 3 detects its compositeness.

blocks.title: Check the base condition before applying the contrapositive

blocks.text: A prime can fail the displayed congruence if the base is divisible by it. For example, 7⁶ mod 7 = 0. A proper common divisor 1 < gcd(a,n) < n proves compositeness, but gcd(a,n) = n does not.

blocks.prompt: Does passing the base-2 test allow you to use Fermat’s theorem with every other base?

explanation.text: No. Passing one necessary test does not establish the prime hypothesis. The example 341 passes base 2 but fails base 3.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.6, pp. 298–299.

units.title: Recognize composites that fool every coprime Fermat base

blocks.text: A Carmichael number is composite and satisfies a^(n−1) ≡ 1 (mod n) for every a relatively prime to n. This shows why simply trying more coprime bases cannot make the basic Fermat test a universal proof of primality.

blocks.title: Verify a Carmichael example using CRT

blocks.text: Take n = 1105 = 5·13·17. If gcd(a,1105) = 1, the base is nonzero modulo each of these primes. Fermat gives powers with periods dividing 4,12,16.
All three numbers divide 1104: 1104 = 4·276 = 12·92 = 16·69. Therefore a¹¹⁰⁴ ≡ 1 modulo 5,13,17.
The primes are pairwise coprime, so their product divides a¹¹⁰⁴ − 1. Thus a¹¹⁰⁴ ≡ 1 (mod 1105) for every allowed a, proving the Carmichael property.

More refined primality tests use extra structure beyond the single Fermat equality. Their probability guarantees require specifying the test and how bases are selected; they do not follow merely from running this equality several times.

blocks.prompt: Does the definition claim 5¹¹⁰⁴ ≡ 1 (mod 1105)?

explanation.text: No. The base 5 is not relatively prime to 1105. In fact it is 0 modulo 5, so that power cannot be 1 modulo 5 or modulo 1105.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.6, pp. 299–300.

units.title: Ask whether one base reaches every nonzero residue

blocks.text: For a prime modulus p, a primitive root r is a nonzero residue whose powers reach all p − 1 nonzero residues. The order of r is the smallest positive exponent d for which rᵈ ≡ 1. A primitive root has order p − 1.

The table contains every residue 1 through 12 exactly once, so 2 is a primitive root modulo 13. At exponent 12 it returns to 1 and repeats. By contrast, powers of 3 modulo 13 cycle 1,3,9,1,…, reaching only three residues. A nonzero base need not be primitive.

blocks.title: One base covers all residues; another covers a subgroup
blocks.description: Modulo 13, base 2 has a 12-step cycle through every nonzero residue. Base 3 has only the three-step cycle 1,3,9.

blocks.text: A theorem guarantees a primitive root for every prime modulus; proving that existence theorem is beyond this unit. For p = 2 the sole nonzero residue 1 is a primitive root with order 1. We are not asserting that every composite modulus has a primitive root.

blocks.prompt: Why is 0 never a primitive root modulo a prime?

explanation.text: All its positive powers are 0, so it cannot generate the nonzero residues. Primitive roots belong to the nonzero multiplicative residues.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.7, p. 300.

units.title: Fix the exponent range to make the logarithm unique

blocks.notation:
For prime p, primitive root r, and 1 ≤ a < p:
logᵣ(a) modulo p is the unique e with 0 ≤ e < p − 1 and rᵉ ≡ a (mod p).
blocks.description: The modulus and base are part of the question. Exponents repeat modulo p − 1.

blocks.title: Read discrete logarithms from the power table

blocks.text: Modulo 13 with base 2, 2⁹ ≡ 5, so log₂(5) = 9. Also 2⁶ ≡ 12, so log₂(12) = 6.
The logarithm of 1 is 0 in our chosen range. Exponent 12 also gives 1, but it is outside the range 0 through 11. Including both endpoints would defeat uniqueness.

All integer exponents representing the same nonzero residue agree modulo p − 1. Logarithms turn residue products into exponent sums modulo p − 1. For example, 5·12 ≡ 8 (mod 13), while 9 + 6 ≡ 3 (mod 12), matching 2³ ≡ 8.

blocks.title: A nonprimitive base changes the problem

blocks.text: With base 3 modulo 13, residue 2 is never reached, so it has no logarithm to that base. Residue 1 repeats every 3 exponents. The existence and uniqueness statement above assumes a primitive root.

blocks.prompt: What is log₂(7) modulo 13? Does the answer mean 2⁷ = 7?

explanation.text: The logarithm is 11, since 2¹¹ mod 13 = 7. It describes a power congruent to 7, not an ordinary real-number logarithm or equality.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.7, p. 300.

units.title: Build a small power table and check for repetitions

blocks.text: This teaching function reuses isPrime from Section 4.3 and normalizedMod from this section. It verifies a small prime modulus and generates powers for exponents 0 through p − 2. A repeated residue before all p − 1 entries are filled means the base is not primitive. It returns a Map from residue to exponent.

blocks.description: Executable JavaScript: powerLogTable(13n,2n).get(5n) returns 9n. powerLogTable(13n,3n) rejects the nonprimitive base.

blocks.text: The modulus is deliberately limited to 10000 for this table-building demonstration. It needs p − 1 multiplications and O(p) stored entries, plus the primality check. Because p can be exponential in its bit length, this is not an efficient general discrete-log algorithm. In contrast, repeated squaring can evaluate a specified power without building the whole table.

blocks.prompt: What does the table contain for p = 2 and r = 1?

explanation.text: One entry: residue 1 maps to exponent 0. There are p − 1 = 1 nonzero residues, and the allowed exponent range contains only 0.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §4.4.7, p. 300; executable companion demonstration.

units.title: Choose a solver and verify its hypotheses first

rows: Are the moduli pairwise coprime? If not, are the conditions compatible?
Is p prime and the base nonzero modulo p before reducing the exponent?
Is the base primitive, and which exponent range is being used?

blocks.prompt: Solve 14x ≡ 8 (mod 20).

explanation.text: gcd(14,20) = 2 divides 8. Reduce to 7x ≡ 4 (mod 10). The inverse of 7 is 3, so x ≡ 2 (mod 10). The two residues modulo 20 are 2 and 12. Both give remainder 8 when multiplied by 14.

blocks.prompt: Find all x with x ≡ 2 (mod 5) and x ≡ 4 (mod 7).

explanation.text: Write x = 2 + 5t. Then 5t ≡ 2 (mod 7), so t ≡ 6. Thus x ≡ 32 (mod 35). Check 32 mod 5 = 2 and 32 mod 7 = 4.

blocks.prompt: Compute 4⁵⁰ mod 7 and log₂(10) modulo 13.

explanation.text: Fermat allows exponent reduction modulo 6: 50 mod 6 = 2, so 4⁵⁰ ≡ 16 ≡ 2 (mod 7). The power table modulo 13 gives log₂(10) = 10.

blocks.prompt: Optional project: independently test the solvers on small moduli. What should a result comparison check?

explanation.text: Enumerate all x from 0 through m − 1 and compare them with the classes returned by solveLinear. For CRT, enumerate 0 through M − 1 for small pairwise coprime moduli and compare the sole solution. Test incompatible shared moduli separately. For each discrete-log entry, independently compute rᵉ mod p and recover the key. Include negative coefficients, zero coefficients, missing inverses, and nonprimitive bases.

blocks.text: These methods connect divisibility, prime factors, Bézout identities, modular arithmetic, and exponent cycles. Sections 4.5 and 4.6 apply this toolkit to concrete congruence applications and cryptography.
Textbook connection: §4.4, pp. 290–300; original mixed practice.
